stimuli.title: Reading comprehension
stimuli.text:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

When economists talk about financial inclusion, they often measure it by counting bank accounts. By that measure, India has made remarkable progress: a large majority of adults now hold an account in their own name. Yet an account that lies dormant does little to change a household's life. A vegetable seller who opens an account but continues to borrow from a moneylender at ruinous rates has been included on paper, not in practice.

The real test of inclusion is use. Does the seller save small amounts regularly? Can she obtain a loan on fair terms when her cart breaks down? Is her family protected by insurance if she falls ill? Each of these questions points to a service that must reach her at a cost she can bear and in a form she trusts.

Trust, more than technology, is often the missing link. Many first-time account holders hesitate to deposit money they cannot see, especially when the nearest branch is several kilometres away and the language on the forms is unfamiliar. Business correspondents, local agents who offer basic banking services in villages, have helped to bridge this distance. When the agent is a familiar face from the same community, customers are more willing to try new products.

Technology has, of course, lowered costs dramatically. A transfer that once required a visit to a branch can now be completed on a basic phone in seconds. But a cheaper channel is valuable only if people are confident using it. Fraud, even when rare, spreads fear quickly; a single story of a neighbour losing savings to a fake call can undo months of patient outreach.

For banks, the lesson is that inclusion is not a target to be reached and then forgotten. It is a relationship that has to be built and renewed, one customer at a time. The institutions that invest in financial literacy, simple products and prompt grievance redressal are likely to find that the small customer, once won over, is also a loyal one.

stimuli.title: Reading comprehension
stimuli.text:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

On a summer afternoon, the temperature in a crowded city centre can be several degrees higher than in the green suburbs only a few kilometres away. Scientists call this the urban heat island effect. Concrete, asphalt and glass absorb the sun's heat during the day and release it slowly at night, so the city never quite cools down. Air conditioners, vehicles and factories add their own waste heat to the mix.

The consequences are more than a matter of comfort. Hot nights prevent the body from recovering after a hot day, and doctors note that elderly people and outdoor workers are especially vulnerable. Electricity demand also climbs as more households switch on coolers and air conditioners, which in turn release more heat outside. In this way, the problem tends to feed on itself.

Trees offer one of the cheapest remedies. A mature tree shades the ground beneath it and cools the surrounding air by releasing water vapour through its leaves. Streets lined with trees can be noticeably cooler than bare streets nearby. Parks, lakes and even rooftop gardens play a similar role. Yet in many growing cities, old trees are cut down to widen roads, and new saplings are planted without any plan to water or protect them, so few survive.

Planners are now experimenting with other ideas as well. Roofs painted white reflect sunlight instead of absorbing it, and some cities have tried lighter-coloured paving. These measures are inexpensive, but they work best when combined with green cover rather than as substitutes for it.

None of this demands new technology. What it demands is that cooling be treated as part of basic urban infrastructure, as important as drains or street lights, rather than as an afterthought once the city has already been built.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: Banks should stop opening new accounts until financial literacy has improved
Moneylenders usually offer fairer terms to small borrowers than banks are able to
Financial inclusion should be judged by how people use banking services, not by how many accounts exist
India has failed to open enough bank accounts for its adult population over the past decade
Technology alone has solved the problem of reaching customers in rural areas
questions.explanation: The passage says an unused account is inclusion 'on paper, not in practice' and that 'the real test of inclusion is use'. It praises the growth in accounts, so it does not say India failed; it says trust, not technology, is the missing link; and it calls moneylender rates ruinous.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why do many first-time account holders hesitate to deposit money?
options: The branch may be far, the forms unfamiliar and the money unseen
Business correspondents refuse to accept very small deposits
They prefer to keep all of their savings in the form of gold
Banks charge a fee on every deposit made by a new customer
Interest rates on savings accounts have fallen in recent years
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says they hesitate to deposit money they cannot see, especially when the branch is several kilometres away and the language on the forms is unfamiliar. Fees, gold and interest rates are never mentioned.

questions.stem: What role do business correspondents play, according to the passage?
options: They offer basic banking in villages through people the community knows
They train branch staff to fill in forms in local languages
They investigate cases of fraud reported by rural customers
They design new digital payment products for the banks
They lend money to villagers at the same rates as moneylenders
questions.explanation: The passage defines business correspondents as local agents who offer basic banking services in villages, and adds that customers trust a familiar face from the same community.

questions.stem: What can be inferred from the statement that a single story of fraud 'can undo months of patient outreach'?
options: Outreach programmes are a waste of a bank's money
Customer confidence is fragile and easily damaged
Banks should stop offering transfers on basic phones
Fraud is the most common problem in rural banking
Most villagers have already lost savings to fraud
questions.explanation: The writer says fraud is rare but spreads fear quickly, so one story can wipe out trust built over months. That shows confidence is fragile. The passage calls fraud rare, so it is not the most common problem, and it does not reject phone transfers or outreach.

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly SIMILAR in meaning to 'ruinous' as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: 'Ruinous rates' are rates so high that they ruin the borrower: devastating. Moderate is close to the opposite, and the others do not describe how harmful the rates are.

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to 'dormant' as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: A dormant account is one that is not used. Its opposite is active. Latent, idle, unused and quiet are all close in meaning to dormant.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT true according to the passage?
options: Prompt grievance redressal can help banks win loyal customers
A familiar local agent makes customers likelier to try products
Insurance is one of the services that inclusion should provide
Most Indian adults now hold a bank account in their own name
Technology has made money transfers costlier for rural users
questions.explanation: The passage says technology has 'lowered costs dramatically', so the statement that technology made transfers costlier is false. Each of the other statements is stated in the passage.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?
options: A History of Indian Banking Law
How to Open a Savings Account
questions.explanation: The passage argues that inclusion goes beyond opening accounts to regular use, trust and service, which 'Beyond the Bank Account' captures. It does not say moneylenders have disappeared or that mobile banking failed, and it gives no instructions or legal history.

questions.stem: Which sentence should come FIRST after the rearrangement?
questions.explanation: The correct order is B F D A E C. B introduces the topic (the monsoon decides farmers' fortunes); F explains what happens when rains are delayed; D brings in micro-irrigation to reduce 'this dependence'; A describes 'these systems'; E gives the problem ('however, their high initial cost'); C draws the conclusion ('therefore').

questions.stem: Which sentence should come SECOND after the rearrangement?
questions.explanation: The order is B F D A E C. F follows B because it explains how the monsoon decides farmers' fortunes: delayed rains push back sowing and cut yields. D cannot come second because 'this dependence' needs F before it.

questions.stem: Which sentence should come FOURTH after the rearrangement?
questions.explanation: The order is B F D A E C. A ('These systems deliver water directly to the roots') must follow D, which names drip and sprinkler systems.

questions.stem: Which sentence should come FIFTH after the rearrangement?
questions.explanation: The order is B F D A E C. After A describes the benefit of micro-irrigation, E introduces the drawback with 'However, their high initial cost'.

questions.stem: Which sentence should come LAST (SIXTH) after the rearrangement?
questions.explanation: The order is B F D A E C. C begins with 'therefore' and offers the solution (subsidies and credit) to the cost problem raised in E, so it closes the paragraph.

questions.stem: Which word fits blank (1) best?
questions.explanation: 'Yet they often find it difficult to borrow' sets up the contrast with 'backbone of many local economies' and leads into the next sentence about collateral. 'Find it eager' and 'find it keen' are ungrammatical, and pleasant or certain contradict the rest of the passage.

questions.stem: Which word fits blank (2) best?
questions.explanation: Banks ask for collateral and audited accounts, which most small traders do not possess (have). That is why they turn to informal lenders. The other verbs do not make sense with collateral and accounts as the object.

questions.stem: Which word fits blank (3) best?
questions.explanation: A guarantee scheme tries to close, or bridge, the gap between small businesses and formal credit. Widen, ignore and create would make the gap worse or leave it as it is.

questions.stem: Which word fits blank (4) best?
questions.explanation: If the government repays part of a defaulted loan, banks carry less risk, so they become more willing to lend. Reluctant and afraid reverse the logic.

questions.stem: Which word fits blank (5) best?
questions.explanation: 'Not a solution for every problem, but they have helped thousands' concedes a limit and then states a benefit. The other words do not fit 'for every problem' with that contrast.

questions.stem: Which word fits blank (6) best?
questions.explanation: A credit history makes the next loan easier to obtain, because the lender can see that the borrower repaid before.

questions.stem:

questions.stem:

questions.stem:

questions.stem:
Which of the following should replace the part in bold to make the sentence correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No improvement'.

Hardly had the train left the station **than it started raining**.
options: than it was starting to rain
questions.explanation: 'Hardly' and 'scarcely' are followed by 'when' (or 'before'), not 'than'. 'No sooner' is the one that takes 'than'.

questions.stem:
Which of the following should replace the part in bold to make the sentence correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No improvement'.

The manager insisted that every employee **attends** the training session.
questions.explanation: After verbs such as insist, suggest and recommend, the that-clause uses 'should' plus the base verb (or the base verb alone): 'insisted that every employee should attend'. 'Attends', 'to attend' and 'attending' are not correct after 'insisted that'.

Two equations, I and II, are given. Solve both and choose the correct relationship between x and y.

II. y² − 3y + 2 = 0

A shopkeeper marks a ceiling fan 40% above its cost price and then allows a discount of 15% on the marked price. If the cost price is ₹2,000, what is his profit?
What is the difference between the compound interest and the simple interest on ₹10,000 for 2 years at 10% per annum, interest compounded annually?
Anil can finish a piece of work in 12 days and Sunil can finish it in 18 days. Working together, in how many days can they finish it?
questions.explanation: Together they do 1/12 + 1/18 = 3/36 + 2/36 = 5/36 of the work per day, so they need 36/5 = 7.2 days.

questions.stem: A train running at 54 km/h crosses a 300 m long platform in 30 seconds. What is the length of the train?
questions.explanation: 54 km/h = 54 × 5/18 = 15 m/s. In 30 seconds the train covers 450 m, which is its own length plus the platform. Train = 450 − 300 = 150 m.

questions.stem: The ratio of the present ages of Meena and her mother is 2 : 5. After 8 years, the ratio will be 1 : 2. What is Meena's present age?
questions.explanation: Let the ages be 2x and 5x. (2x + 8) ÷ (5x + 8) = 1/2, so 4x + 16 = 5x + 8 and x = 8. Meena is 2 × 8 = 16.

questions.stem: The average weight of 6 parcels is 15 kg. When a seventh parcel is added, the average weight becomes 16 kg. What does the seventh parcel weigh?
questions.explanation: Total of six = 6 × 15 = 90 kg. Total of seven = 7 × 16 = 112 kg. The seventh parcel weighs 112 − 90 = 22 kg.

questions.stem: Ravi and Kiran start a business with ₹40,000 and ₹60,000 respectively. After 6 months, Ravi invests another ₹20,000. At the end of the year the profit is ₹55,000. What is Ravi's share?
A 45-litre mixture contains juice and water in the ratio 4 : 1. How much water must be added so that juice makes up 60% of the new mixture?
questions.explanation: Juice = 36 L. For juice to be 60% of the mixture, the total must be 36 ÷ 0.6 = 60 L. Add 60 − 45 = 15 litres of water.

questions.stem: A bag contains 4 red balls and 6 blue balls. Two balls are drawn at random. What is the probability that both are red?
questions.explanation: Ways to choose 2 red = 4C2 = 6. Ways to choose any 2 = 10C2 = 45. Probability = 6/45 = 2/15.

questions.stem: A boat's speed in still water is 15 km/h and the speed of the stream is 3 km/h. How long will the boat take to go 36 km downstream and come back?
questions.explanation: Downstream speed = 18 km/h, so 36 ÷ 18 = 2 hours. Upstream speed = 12 km/h, so 36 ÷ 12 = 3 hours. Total = 5 hours.

questions.stem:

A statement is followed by two conclusions, I and II. Assume the statement is true and decide which conclusion(s) definitely follow.

Statement: K < L ≤ M = N ≥ O > P

I. M > O

II. M = O
questions.explanation: M = N ≥ O, so M ≥ O. Neither M > O nor M = O is certain on its own, but one of them must be true, and together they cover every case. Either I or II follows.

questions.stem:
A statement is followed by two conclusions, I and II. Assume the statement is true and decide which conclusion(s) definitely follow.

Statement: S ≤ T < U ≥ V = W > X

I. T < V

II. X < U
questions.explanation: I: T < U and U ≥ V point in opposite directions, so T and V cannot be compared. II: X < W = V ≤ U gives X < U, true. Only II follows.

questions.stem:
Some statements are followed by two conclusions, I and II. Take the statements to be true even if they seem to differ from commonly known facts, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow.

Statements: All banks are offices. Some offices are branches.

I. Some banks are branches.

II. All offices are banks.
questions.explanation: The branches that are offices need not be banks, so I is not certain. 'All banks are offices' does not mean all offices are banks, so II does not follow. Neither follows.

questions.stem:
Some statements are followed by two conclusions, I and II. Take the statements to be true even if they seem to differ from commonly known facts, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow.

Statements: All pens are pencils. All pencils are erasers.

I. All pens are erasers.

II. Some erasers are pens.
questions.explanation: All pens are pencils and all pencils are erasers, so all pens are erasers (I). Since every pen is an eraser, some erasers are pens (II). Both follow.

questions.stem:
Some statements are followed by two conclusions, I and II. Take the statements to be true even if they seem to differ from commonly known facts, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow.

Statements: Some cards are coins. No coin is a note.

I. Some cards are not notes.

II. Some notes are cards.
questions.explanation: The cards that are coins cannot be notes, so some cards are not notes (I). Nothing links notes to the other cards, so II is only a possibility. Only I follows.

questions.stem:
Some statements are followed by two conclusions, I and II. Take the statements to be true even if they seem to differ from commonly known facts, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow.

Statements: All files are folders. Some folders are boxes.

I. Some files are boxes.

II. No file is a box.
questions.explanation: Neither conclusion is certain on its own: files may or may not overlap boxes. But I and II are complementary, about the same two terms, and one of them must be true. Either I or II follows.

questions.stem: Who sits at the extreme right end of the row?
questions.explanation: Final arrangement, left to right: D, F, A, G, C, B, E. G is 4th (middle), A is 3rd, B is 6th (two between A and B), E is 7th, so D takes the other end, 1st. C cannot sit next to D, so C is 5th and F is 2nd. E is at the right end.

questions.stem: How many persons sit between D and C?
questions.explanation: Final arrangement, left to right: D, F, A, G, C, B, E. G is 4th (middle), A is 3rd, B is 6th (two between A and B), E is 7th, so D takes the other end, 1st. C cannot sit next to D, so C is 5th and F is 2nd. D is 1st and C is 5th, so F, A and G sit between them.

questions.stem: Who sits immediately to the left of B?
questions.explanation: Final arrangement, left to right: D, F, A, G, C, B, E. G is 4th (middle), A is 3rd, B is 6th (two between A and B), E is 7th, so D takes the other end, 1st. C cannot sit next to D, so C is 5th and F is 2nd. Facing north, left is towards the 1st seat, so the person immediately left of B (6th) is C (5th).

questions.stem: Which of the following pairs sit next to each other?
questions.explanation: Final arrangement, left to right: D, F, A, G, C, B, E. G is 4th (middle), A is 3rd, B is 6th (two between A and B), E is 7th, so D takes the other end, 1st. C cannot sit next to D, so C is 5th and F is 2nd. F (2nd) and A (3rd) are neighbours; none of the other pairs are.

questions.stem: Who sits third to the left of B?
questions.explanation: Final arrangement, left to right: D, F, A, G, C, B, E. G is 4th (middle), A is 3rd, B is 6th (two between A and B), E is 7th, so D takes the other end, 1st. C cannot sit next to D, so C is 5th and F is 2nd. B is 6th, so third to the left is the 3rd seat, A.

questions.stem: Who sits opposite R?
questions.explanation: Clockwise from P (facing the centre, a person's left is the next seat clockwise): P, T, R, W, Q, V, S, U. Q is opposite P; T is P's immediate left and R second to the left; U must be P's other neighbour, so S is next to U; W is Q's immediate right; V takes the last seat. R is in the 3rd seat clockwise and S is four seats away, in the 7th.

questions.stem: Who sits immediately to the left of Q?
questions.explanation: Clockwise from P (facing the centre, a person's left is the next seat clockwise): P, T, R, W, Q, V, S, U. Q is opposite P; T is P's immediate left and R second to the left; U must be P's other neighbour, so S is next to U; W is Q's immediate right; V takes the last seat. Q's immediate left is the next seat clockwise, V. W is on Q's right.

questions.stem: Counting clockwise from T, how many persons sit between T and V?
questions.explanation: Clockwise from P (facing the centre, a person's left is the next seat clockwise): P, T, R, W, Q, V, S, U. Q is opposite P; T is P's immediate left and R second to the left; U must be P's other neighbour, so S is next to U; W is Q's immediate right; V takes the last seat. Clockwise from T: R, W, Q, then V. Three persons sit between them.

questions.stem: What is the position of U with respect to W?
options: Second to the left of W
Second to the right of W
Third to the right of W
questions.explanation: Clockwise from P (facing the centre, a person's left is the next seat clockwise): P, T, R, W, Q, V, S, U. Q is opposite P; T is P's immediate left and R second to the left; U must be P's other neighbour, so S is next to U; W is Q's immediate right; V takes the last seat. W is in the 4th seat and U in the 8th, four seats apart, so U sits opposite W.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true?
options: S sits second to the right of P
R is an immediate neighbour of P
V sits immediately to the left of S
Q sits between W and R
questions.explanation: Clockwise from P (facing the centre, a person's left is the next seat clockwise): P, T, R, W, Q, V, S, U. Q is opposite P; T is P's immediate left and R second to the left; U must be P's other neighbour, so S is next to U; W is Q's immediate right; V takes the last seat. P's right is anticlockwise: U, then S, so S is second to the right of P. T is opposite V, R is not next to P, S's immediate left is U, and Q sits between W and V.

questions.stem: Who lives on floor 2?
questions.explanation: Floors 1 to 5: M (Guava), K (Apple), N (Mango), J (Banana), L (Grapes). L is on 5, so N is on 3. K is immediately above M, which fits only on floors 2 and 1, leaving J on 4; the Mango lover is below J, so N likes Mango. M (floor 1) likes Guava, K takes Apple, and L, not liking Banana, takes Grapes.

questions.stem: Which fruit does J like?
questions.explanation: Floors 1 to 5: M (Guava), K (Apple), N (Mango), J (Banana), L (Grapes). L is on 5, so N is on 3. K is immediately above M, which fits only on floors 2 and 1, leaving J on 4; the Mango lover is below J, so N likes Mango. M (floor 1) likes Guava, K takes Apple, and L, not liking Banana, takes Grapes.

questions.stem: How many persons live between M and J?
questions.explanation: Floors 1 to 5: M (Guava), K (Apple), N (Mango), J (Banana), L (Grapes). L is on 5, so N is on 3. K is immediately above M, which fits only on floors 2 and 1, leaving J on 4; the Mango lover is below J, so N likes Mango. M (floor 1) likes Guava, K takes Apple, and L, not liking Banana, takes Grapes. M is on floor 1 and J on floor 4, so K and N live between them.

questions.stem: Who likes Grapes?
questions.explanation: Floors 1 to 5: M (Guava), K (Apple), N (Mango), J (Banana), L (Grapes). L is on 5, so N is on 3. K is immediately above M, which fits only on floors 2 and 1, leaving J on 4; the Mango lover is below J, so N likes Mango. M (floor 1) likes Guava, K takes Apple, and L, not liking Banana, takes Grapes.

questions.stem: Which of the following combinations is correct?
questions.explanation: Floors 1 to 5: M (Guava), K (Apple), N (Mango), J (Banana), L (Grapes). L is on 5, so N is on 3. K is immediately above M, which fits only on floors 2 and 1, leaving J on 4; the Mango lover is below J, so N likes Mango. M (floor 1) likes Guava, K takes Apple, and L, not liking Banana, takes Grapes.

questions.stem: In a certain code language, BANK is written as CBOL. How is LOAN written in that code?
questions.explanation: Each letter moves one place forward: B→C, A→B, N→O, K→L. So L→M, O→P, A→B, N→O gives MPBO.

questions.stem: In a certain code, 'save money daily' is written as 'ka pi to', 'money is power' as 'ru pi se', and 'daily power cut' as 'to se mo'. What is the code for 'save'?
questions.explanation: 'Money' is in the first two sentences and their common code is 'pi'. 'Daily' is in the first and third and their common code is 'to'. That leaves 'ka' for 'save'.

questions.stem: If LOCKER is coded as REKCOL, how is CLERK coded in the same way?
questions.explanation: The code writes the word backwards: LOCKER becomes REKCOL. CLERK backwards is KRELC.

questions.stem: Pointing to a woman in a photograph, Ramesh said, 'She is the only daughter of my paternal grandfather's only son.' How is the woman related to Ramesh?
questions.explanation: His paternal grandfather (his father's father) has only one son, so that son must be Ramesh's father. The only daughter of Ramesh's father is Ramesh's sister.

questions.stem: K is the son of L. L is the daughter of M. N is the husband of M. How is N related to K?
questions.explanation: L is K's mother, and M is L's mother. N, M's husband, is L's father, so N is K's mother's father: his maternal grandfather.

questions.stem: P is the mother of Q. Q is the sister of R. R is the father of S. How is P related to S?
questions.explanation: Q and R are siblings, so P is R's mother too. R is S's father, so P is S's grandmother.

questions.stem: Sunita walks 12 m south, turns left and walks 7 m, then turns left again and walks 12 m. How far and in which direction is she from her starting point?
questions.explanation: Facing south, a left turn faces east, so she walks 7 m east; facing east, a left turn faces north, so she walks 12 m back north. The north and south cancel, leaving her 7 m east of the start.

questions.stem: Vikram is facing west. He turns 45° clockwise and then a further 180° clockwise. Which direction is he facing now?
questions.explanation: From west, 45° clockwise is north-west. A further 180° turns him to face the opposite way, south-east.

questions.stem: From point X, Raju walks 8 km south and then 6 km west. What is the shortest distance between Raju and point X?
questions.explanation: The two legs are at right angles, so the distance is √(8² + 6²) = √100 = 10 km.

questions.stem: In a queue of 52 people at a bank counter, Farida is 19th from the front. What is her position from the back?
questions.explanation: Position from the back = total − position from the front + 1 = 52 − 19 + 1 = 34th.

questions.stem: In a class, Arjun ranks 9th from the top and 31st from the bottom. How many students are in the class?
questions.explanation: Total = 9 + 31 − 1 = 39, since Arjun is counted in both ranks.

questions.stem: If the letters of the word PLANET are arranged in alphabetical order, which letter will be third from the right?
questions.explanation: Alphabetical order: A, E, L, N, P, T. Counting from the right: T, P, N. The third is N.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why does a city centre stay warm at night?
options: Suburbs send their warm air towards the centre in the evening
Night-time traffic is heavier than daytime traffic in cities
Street lights produce large amounts of heat after sunset
Tall buildings block the cool winds that blow in from the sea
Concrete, asphalt and glass release stored daytime heat slowly
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says these materials absorb the sun's heat during the day and release it slowly at night, so the city never quite cools down. Winds, street lights and suburbs are not given as causes.

questions.stem: What does the writer mean by saying that the problem 'tends to feed on itself'?
options: Cities keep growing larger because people move in from villages
Coping with the heat, through air conditioners, produces still more heat
Doctors cannot treat heat illness without using more electricity
Outdoor workers lose income on hot days and cannot buy coolers
Trees planted in cities need more water as the climate warms
questions.explanation: The sentence before says more coolers and air conditioners are switched on, 'which in turn release more heat outside'. The response to heat adds to the heat, a self-reinforcing loop.

questions.stem: Which groups does the passage name as especially vulnerable to hot nights?
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'doctors note that elderly people and outdoor workers are especially vulnerable'.

questions.stem: Why, according to the passage, do few newly planted saplings survive in many growing cities?
options: Most cities plant species that are not native to the region
Hot nights stop young trees from releasing water vapour
Residents remove them because they block shop signs
The soil in city centres is too poor for young trees to grow
They are planted without any plan to water or protect them
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says new saplings are planted 'without any plan to water or protect them, so few survive'. Soil, signs and species are not mentioned.

questions.stem: What is the writer's view of white roofs and lighter paving?
options: They work better than trees and should be the first priority
They need advanced technology that cities do not yet have
They have been tried and shown to make streets warmer
They are useful but should support green cover, not replace it
They are too costly for most Indian cities to adopt widely
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 calls them inexpensive and says they 'work best when combined with green cover rather than as substitutes for it'. The final paragraph says no new technology is needed.

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly SIMILAR in meaning to 'vulnerable' as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: Vulnerable people are easily harmed by the heat: susceptible. Resistant is the opposite, and the others do not fit.

questions.stem: Which word is most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to 'afterthought' as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: An afterthought is something considered only later, as an extra. Its opposite is a priority, something considered first. Addition, postscript, appendix and supplement are all close in meaning to afterthought.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the passage?
options: To explain how air conditioners work and how to choose one
To describe the history of tree planting in Indian cities
To argue that cooling should be planned as basic city infrastructure
To show that the urban heat island effect has been exaggerated
To criticise doctors for ignoring the effects of heat on health
questions.explanation: The passage explains the heat island effect and its harm, then argues in its last paragraph that cooling must be treated as basic infrastructure, like drains and street lights.

questions.stem: Which sentence should come FIRST after the rearrangement?
questions.explanation: The correct order is C E A F D B. C sets the scene (libraries were once the main gateway to books); E gives the assumption that smartphones would make them irrelevant; A begins 'Instead' and says they reinvented themselves; F lists what they now host; D picks up 'the exam coaching sessions'; B concludes.

questions.stem: Which sentence should come SECOND after the rearrangement?
questions.explanation: The order is C E A F D B. E follows C: libraries were once central, then smartphones made people expect them to become irrelevant. A ('Instead') needs E's assumption before it.

questions.stem: Which sentence should come THIRD after the rearrangement?
questions.explanation: The order is C E A F D B. A begins 'Instead', contradicting E's expectation that libraries would become irrelevant.

questions.stem: Which sentence should come FIFTH after the rearrangement?
questions.explanation: The order is C E A F D B. D refers to 'the exam coaching sessions', which F introduces, so D comes right after F.

questions.stem: Which sentence should come LAST (SIXTH) after the rearrangement?
questions.explanation: The order is C E A F D B. B ('Far from disappearing, the library may simply be changing its shape') sums up the paragraph, so it comes last.

questions.stem: Which word fits blank (1) best?
questions.explanation: A crisis 'has struck' means it has happened suddenly. Families think about insurance only after that. The other verbs do not collocate with crisis here.

questions.stem: Which word fits blank (2) best?
questions.explanation: 'Yet a health policy is often seen as an unnecessary expense' contrasts with the hospital bill that wipes out savings. 'Unnecessary necessity' contradicts itself, and the other words make no sense.

questions.stem: Which word fits blank (3) best?
questions.explanation: The colon explains the blank: you pay every year and may never claim, so the benefits are not seen, invisible. Immediate, obvious and guaranteed say the opposite.

questions.stem: Which word fits blank (4) best?
questions.explanation: Agents who explain policies simply can dispel (remove) the doubt. Deepen, spread and confirm would increase it.

questions.stem: Which word fits blank (5) best?
questions.explanation: Regulators want claims settled more promptly, because 'a delayed payment' harms trust, as the rest of the sentence says.

questions.stem: Which word fits blank (6) best?
questions.explanation: A delayed payment does more to erode (wear away) trust than any advertisement can build. Build, restore and earn would remove the contrast with 'than any advertisement can build'.

questions.stem:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.

The scientist's findings were initially met with ........, but later experiments confirmed her results.
questions.explanation: 'But later experiments confirmed' signals a contrast: at first people doubted the findings. Scepticism means doubt. The other options would not contrast with confirmation.

questions.stem:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.

Priya is so ........ that she double-checks every figure before sending a report.
questions.explanation: Double-checking every figure shows great care: meticulous. The other words describe the opposite.

questions.stem:
Choose the pair of words that best fills the blanks.

The bridge was ........ (i) after engineers found cracks, and traffic was ........ (ii) to an older road.
questions.explanation: Cracks lead to the bridge being closed, and traffic is then diverted to another road. 'Opened' contradicts the cracks, and 'invited', 'banned to' and 'attracted to' do not fit traffic being sent elsewhere.

questions.stem:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.

The minister's speech was ........; it lasted two hours but said very little.
questions.explanation: A long speech that says little is verbose (wordy). Concise, brief, pointed and crisp all mean the opposite.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence and find the part that contains an error. If there is no error, choose E.

One of my friends (A) / are working (B) / as a clerk (C) / in a public sector bank. (D) / No error (E)
questions.explanation: The subject is 'one', which is singular, so the verb should be 'is working'. 'Of my friends' does not change the subject.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence and find the part that contains an error. If there is no error, choose E.

The informations (A) / given by the customer (B) / was checked (C) / by the officer. (D) / No error (E)
questions.explanation: 'Information' is an uncountable noun and has no plural form, so it should be 'The information'. The singular 'was checked' is then correct.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence and find the part that contains an error. If there is no error, choose E.

He likes Pune very much (A) / and has been living (B) / in the city (C) / since five years. (D) / No error (E)
questions.explanation: 'Since' is used with a point in time (since 2020) and 'for' with a period (for five years). It should be 'for five years'.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence and find the part that contains an error. If there is no error, choose E.

The doctor advised him (A) / to avoid sweets (B) / and take (C) / a walk every morning. (D) / No error (E)
questions.explanation: The sentence is correct. 'Advised him to avoid ... and (to) take' is a parallel pair of infinitives, and the second 'to' may be left out.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence and find the part that contains an error. If there is no error, choose E.

The manager along with (A) / his team members (B) / are attending (C) / the conference in Delhi. (D) / No error (E)
questions.explanation: When a subject is joined by 'along with', 'as well as' or 'together with', the verb agrees with the first subject. 'The manager' is singular, so it should be 'is attending'.

questions.stem:
Which of the following should replace the part in bold to make the sentence correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No improvement'.

No sooner did the bell ring **when the students rushed out** of the classroom.
options: that the students were rushing out
questions.explanation: 'No sooner' is always followed by 'than': 'No sooner did the bell ring than the students rushed out'.

questions.stem:
Which of the following should replace the part in bold to make the sentence correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No improvement'.

She is one of those officers who **always tries** to help customers.
questions.explanation: In 'one of those officers who ...', the relative pronoun 'who' refers to 'officers' (plural), so the verb is plural: 'who always try'. 'Has always tried' and 'is always trying' are singular.

questions.stem:

35% of 640 + 2/5 of 450 = ?
questions.explanation: 35% of 640 = 224 and 2/5 of 450 = 180, so the total is 404.

What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following number series?

6, 7, 11, 20, 36, ?

2, 2, 4, 12, 48, ?
questions.explanation: Multiply by 1, 2, 3, 4, then 5: 48 × 5 = 240.

2880, 1440, 480, 120, 24, ?
questions.explanation: Divide by 2, 3, 4, 5, then 6: 24 ÷ 6 = 4.

4, 9, 25, 49, 121, ?
questions.explanation: These are the squares of consecutive primes: 2², 3², 5², 7², 11². Next is 13² = 169.

questions.stem:
Two equations, I and II, are given. Solve both and choose the correct relationship between x and y.

I. x² − 13x + 42 = 0

II. y² − 11y + 30 = 0
options: x = y or no relation can be established

questions.stem:
Two equations, I and II, are given. Solve both and choose the correct relationship between x and y.

I. x² + 11x + 30 = 0

II. y² + 5y + 6 = 0
options: x = y or no relation can be established
questions.explanation: I: x = −5 or −6. II: y = −2 or −3. Every value of x is less than every value of y, so x < y.

questions.stem:
Two equations, I and II, are given. Solve both and choose the correct relationship between x and y.

I. x² − x − 12 = 0

II. y² − 2y − 8 = 0
options: x = y or no relation can be established
questions.explanation: I: (x − 4)(x + 3) = 0, so x = 4 or −3. II: (y − 4)(y + 2) = 0, so y = 4 or −2. x = 4 equals y = 4 and exceeds −2, but x = −3 is less than both. No single relationship holds.

questions.stem:
Two equations, I and II, are given. Solve both and choose the correct relationship between x and y.

I. 3x² − 10x + 8 = 0

II. y² − 6y + 8 = 0
options: x = y or no relation can be established

questions.stem:
Two equations, I and II, are given. Solve both and choose the correct relationship between x and y.

I. x² − 15x + 56 = 0

II. y² − 9y + 18 = 0
options: x = y or no relation can be established
questions.explanation: I: x = 7 or 8. II: y = 3 or 6. Every value of x is greater than every value of y, so x > y.

questions.stem: How many passengers in all used the five stations in February?
By what percentage did the number of passengers at station E fall from January to February?
questions.explanation: E fell from 90 to 72 thousand, a fall of 18. 18 ÷ 90 × 100 = 20%.

questions.stem: What is the ratio of station C's total passengers over the two months to station D's total over the two months?
At how many of the five stations did the number of passengers increase from January to February?
questions.explanation: A (45 to 54), C (75 to 90) and D (30 to 36) rose; B and E fell. That is 3 stations.

questions.stem: February passengers at station A are what percentage of January passengers at station C?
How much does the family spend on food each month?
By how much does the monthly rent exceed the monthly spending on education?
questions.explanation: Rent 25% and education 15% differ by 10% of ₹48,000 = ₹4,800.

questions.stem: If the family's income rises by 25% and savings stay at the same percentage of income, what will its monthly savings be?
Spending on transport and others together is what percentage of spending on food?
questions.explanation: Transport 10% + others 8% = 18% of income. Food is 30%. 18 ÷ 30 × 100 = 60%.

questions.stem: If the budget were drawn as a pie chart, what would be the central angle of the education sector?
questions.explanation: Education is 15% of 360° = 54°.

questions.stem: By selling a mobile phone for ₹9,000, a dealer loses 10%. At what price should he sell it to gain 15%?
questions.explanation: ₹9,000 is 90% of the cost price, so the cost price is ₹10,000. For a 15% gain he must sell at ₹11,500.

questions.stem: What amount will ₹8,000 grow to in 2 years at 5% per annum, compounded annually?

Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 12 hours and 20 hours respectively, while pipe C can empty the full tank in 15 hours. If all three are opened together on an empty tank, how long will it take to fill it?
questions.explanation: Net filling per hour = 1/12 + 1/20 − 1/15 = 5/60 + 3/60 − 4/60 = 4/60 = 1/15, so the tank fills in 15 hours.

questions.stem: A car covers the first 120 km of a journey at 60 km/h and the next 120 km at 40 km/h. What is its average speed for the whole journey?
questions.explanation: Time = 120/60 + 120/40 = 2 + 3 = 5 hours for 240 km. Average speed = 240 ÷ 5 = 48 km/h, not the simple average of 50.

questions.stem: The sum of the present ages of a father and his son is 56 years. Four years ago, the father was three times as old as the son. What is the father's present age?
In an election between two candidates, the winner received 58% of the valid votes and won by 4,800 votes. How many valid votes were cast?

questions.stem: ₹8,800 is divided among Nisha, Omkar and Preeti in the ratio 4 : 5 : 2. How much more does Omkar get than Preeti?

questions.explanation: Total work = 12 × 15 = 180 man-days. 180 ÷ 9 = 20 men.

questions.stem:

questions.stem:

questions.explanation: The statements do not link rivers and ponds, so neither conclusion is certain on its own. But I and II are complementary, about the same two terms, so one of them must be true. Either I or II follows.

questions.stem:

If MONDAY is coded as NPOEBZ, how is FRIDAY coded?
questions.explanation: Each letter moves one place forward: M→N, O→P and so on. FRIDAY becomes GSJEBZ.

questions.stem: In a certain code, 'work hard now' is written as 'li ma ta', 'now or never' as 'ta su re', and 'hard and fast' as 'ma ko pa'. What is the code for 'work'?
questions.explanation: 'Now' is common to the first two sentences, code 'ta'. 'Hard' is common to the first and third, code 'ma'. So 'work' is 'li'.

questions.stem: Introducing a man, Pooja said, 'His wife is the only daughter of my mother.' How is the man related to Pooja?
questions.explanation: The only daughter of Pooja's mother is Pooja herself. So the man's wife is Pooja, and he is her husband.

questions.stem: M is the son of N. N is the wife of O. O is the brother of P, and P is a woman. How is P related to M?
questions.explanation: N is M's mother and O, her husband, is M's father. P is O's sister, so P is M's aunt (father's sister).

questions.stem: X and Y are sisters. Z is the father of X. W is the only son of Z. How is Y related to W?
questions.explanation: X and Y are sisters and Z is X's father, so Z is Y's father too. W is Z's son, so Y is W's sister.

questions.stem: Mohan walks 12 m west, then turns left and walks 5 m. How far is he from his starting point?
questions.explanation: Turning left from west means walking south. The two legs are at right angles, so the distance is √(12² + 5²) = √169 = 13 m.

questions.stem: Deepa is facing south. She turns left, then left again, then right. Which direction is she facing now?
questions.explanation: Facing south, a left turn faces east; another left faces north; a right turn from north faces east.

questions.stem: Point A is 5 km north of point B, and point C is 5 km east of point B. In which direction is A from C?
questions.explanation: With B at the origin, A is 5 km north and C is 5 km east. To go from C to A you move west and north, so A is north-west of C.

questions.stem: In a queue, Sneha is 12th from the front and Raj is 18th from the back. Four people stand between them, and Sneha is ahead of Raj. How many people are in the queue?
questions.explanation: With four people between them, Raj is 12 + 5 = 17th from the front. Total = 17 + 18 − 1 = 34.

questions.stem: Amit is heavier than Bharat but lighter than Chirag. Dinesh is heavier than Chirag. Eshan is the lightest of the five. Who is the heaviest?
questions.explanation: Bharat < Amit < Chirag < Dinesh, and Eshan is the lightest. Dinesh is the heaviest.

questions.stem: Which letter is 7th to the right of the 12th letter from the left in the English alphabet?
questions.explanation: The 12th letter from the left is L. Seven places to the right of L is the 19th letter, S.

He did not knew (A) / that the bank (B) / would be closed (C) / on Saturday. (D) / No error (E)
questions.explanation: After the auxiliary 'did', the main verb is in its base form: 'did not know'.

The new policy, (A) / between you and I, (B) / is unlikely (C) / to succeed. (D) / No error (E)
questions.explanation: 'Between' is a preposition, so the pronouns after it take the object form: 'between you and me'.

questions.stem:

The cashier counted (A) / the notes carefully (B) / before handing them (C) / to the customer. (D) / No error (E)
questions.explanation: The sentence is correct. 'Before' is followed by the -ing form (handing), and 'them' refers to the notes.

questions.explanation: In a first conditional, the if-clause takes the simple present and the main clause takes 'will': 'If he works hard, he will clear the exam'.

questions.stem: How many applications were approved in all five districts together?
questions.explanation: Pune 60% of 400 = 240; Nashik 72% of 250 = 180; Nagpur 54% of 500 = 270; Thane 45% of 600 = 270; Satara 80% of 200 = 160. Total 1,120.

questions.stem: By how many does the number of rejected applications in Thane exceed the number rejected in Pune?
questions.explanation: Thane rejected 600 − 270 = 330. Pune rejected 400 − 240 = 160. Difference = 170.

questions.stem: Which two districts approved the same number of applications?
questions.explanation: Nagpur approved 54% of 500 = 270 and Thane approved 45% of 600 = 270.

The price of tea falls by 20%. By what percentage can a family increase its consumption of tea without changing its spending on tea?
questions.explanation: Increase = fall ÷ (100 − fall) × 100 = 20 ÷ 80 × 100 = 25%. For example, ₹100 that bought 1 kg now buys 1.25 kg.

questions.stem: A train 180 m long overtakes a man walking at 6 km/h in the same direction in 12 seconds. What is the speed of the train?
questions.explanation: Relative speed = 180 ÷ 12 = 15 m/s = 54 km/h. Moving in the same direction, train speed = 54 + 6 = 60 km/h.

questions.stem: A can do a job in 20 days and B in 30 days. They work together for 6 days, after which A leaves. In how many more days will B finish the job?
questions.explanation: Together they do 1/20 + 1/30 = 1/12 per day, so 6 days finish 6/12 = 1/2 of the job. B does the other half alone in 30 × 1/2 = 15 days.

questions.explanation: Tallest to shortest: X, U, Z, W, Y, V. X > U > Z and Z > W > Y. Only two are taller than Z, so they are X and U. V is the shortest, so W and Y come next in that order.

questions.stem: How many persons are shorter than W?

questions.stem: Who is the second shortest?
questions.explanation: Tallest to shortest: X, U, Z, W, Y, V. X > U > Z and Z > W > Y. Only two are taller than Z, so they are X and U. V is the shortest, so W and Y come next in that order.

questions.stem: If X is 180 cm tall and V is 150 cm tall, which of the following could be W's height?
questions.explanation: Tallest to shortest: X, U, Z, W, Y, V. X > U > Z and Z > W > Y. Only two are taller than Z, so they are X and U. V is the shortest, so W and Y come next in that order. W is shorter than X and taller than V, and all heights differ, so W is strictly between 150 and 180 cm. Only 162 cm fits.
